claim: Nucleosomes directly block access of CRISPR/Cas9 to DNA.
source: We recently found that nucleosomes directly block access of CRISPR/Cas9 to DNA (Horlbeck et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Horlbeck et al., 2016

claim: A comprehensive algorithm incorporating chromatin, position, and sequence features can accurately predict highly effective sgRNAs for CRISPRi and CRISPRa.
source: Here, we build on this observation with a comprehensive algorithm that incorporates chromatin, position, and sequence features to accurately predict highly effective single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) for targeting nuclease-dead Cas9-mediated transcriptional repression (CRISPRi) and activation (CRISPRa).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the machine learning approach and validation screens described in the manuscript

claim: The large majority of sgRNAs in the CRISPRi v2 library are highly active.
source: A CRISPRi screen for essential genes in K562 cells demonstrates that the large majority of sgRNAs are highly active.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the K562 essential gene screen

claim: CRISPRi does not exhibit detectable non-specific toxicity observed with CRISPR nuclease approaches.
source: We also find CRISPRi does not exhibit any detectable non-specific toxicity recently observed with CRISPR nuclease approaches.
evidence: Supported by experimental comparison of CRISPRi and CRISPR nuclease at the BCR amplicon

claim: Over 90% of essential genes can be detected with minimal false positives using a compact 5 sgRNA/gene library.
source: Precision-recall analysis shows that we detect over 90% of essential genes with minimal false positives using a compact 5 sgRNA/gene library.
evidence: Supported by precision-recall analysis data presented in the manuscript

claim: Nucleosomes provide a direct and profound impediment to Cas9 access to DNA.
source: We and others recently found that nucleosomes provide a direct and profound impediment to Cas9 access to DNA (Hinz et al., 2015; Horlbeck et al., 2016; Isaac et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Nucleosome occupancy is predictive of Cas9 activity complementary to and independent of previously described sgRNA sequence features.
source: We found that nucleosome occupancy was predictive of Cas9 activity complementary to and independent of previously described sgRNA sequence features (Chari et al., 2015; Doench et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations and the machine learning analysis in the manuscript

claim: Strong nucleosome-dependent phasing is observed downstream of the FANTOM consortium-annotated transcription start site (TSS).
source: These observations, along with the strong nucleosome-dependent phasing observed downstream of the FANTOM consortium-annotated transcription start site (TSS) (FANTOM Consortium and the RIKEN PMI and CLST (DGT) et al., 2014; Horlbeck et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to FANTOM consortium and Horlbeck et al.

claim: The machine learning pipeline was trained on data collected from 30 CRISPRi and 9 CRISPRa screens.
source: To test this, we developed a comprehensive machine learning pipeline trained on data collected from 30 CRISPRi and 9 CRISPRa screens.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript

claim: The resulting models were highly predictive of sgRNA efficacy.
source: We found that the resulting models were highly predictive of sgRNA efficacy and strongly weighted nucleosome positioning and specific sequence features.
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis and cross-validation data

claim: The models strongly weighted nucleosome positioning and specific sequence features.
source: We found that the resulting models were highly predictive of sgRNA efficacy and strongly weighted nucleosome positioning and specific sequence features.
evidence: Supported by feature contribution analysis shown in Figure 1C

claim: The hCRISPRi-v2 library identified over 2100 essential genes with high statistical confidence.
source: We identified over 2100 essential genes with high statistical confidence, significantly improving upon our CRISPRi v1 library (Gilbert et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by experimental screen data

claim: The hCRISPRi-v2 library shows increased discrimination of gold standard essential and non-essential genes compared to v1.
source: precision-recall analysis showed increased discrimination of gold standard essential and non-essential genes with both 10 sgRNA/gene and 5 sgRNA/gene hCRISPRi-v2 libraries (Hart et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by precision-recall analysis data

claim: A large majority of the hCRISPRi-v2 sgRNAs targeting known essential genes produced robust growth phenotypes.
source: A large majority of the hCRISPRi-v2 sgRNAs targeting known essential genes produced robust growth phenotypes, a key advance over previous CRISPRi libraries (Evers et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by experimental screen data and comparison to Evers et al.

claim: The algorithm can accurately predict sgRNA activity for data from screens performed with an independently designed library and in different cell types.
source: our algorithm can accurately predict sgRNA activity for data from screens performed with an independently designed library and in different cell types.
evidence: Supported by analysis of Evers et al. data

claim: CRISPRi enables inducible, reversible, and homogenous manipulation of gene expression.
source: our previous findings that CRISPRi enables inducible, reversible, and homogenous manipulation of gene expression (Gilbert et al., 2014; Mandegar et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The hCRISPRa-v2 screen identified 60% more genes that modify growth rates upon overexpression than the v1 screen.
source: We also conducted a screen for genes that modify growth rates upon overexpression with our hCRISPRa-v2 and found this identified 60% more genes, with greater enrichment for previously established classes of hit genes, than our version 1 CRISPRa screen.
evidence: Supported by experimental screen data

claim: The CRISPRi activity dataset contains activity scores for 18,380 sgRNAs targeting 1,539 high-confidence hit genes.
source: we turned to our recently described CRISPRi activity dataset (Horlbeck et al., 2016) in which we integrated data from 30 CRISPRi screens to select 1,539 high-confidence hit genes, and normalized the phenotypes for sgRNAs targeting each gene to the strongest sgRNAs for that gene, resulting in 'activity scores' for 18,380 sgRNAs.
evidence: Directly stated description of the training dataset

claim: The model achieved a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.80 in cross-validation.
source: By performing regression on a training set of only 80% of the genes in the CRISPRi activity dataset, we found that the model was highly predictive of activity in the test set comprising the remaining 20% of the genes, with a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.80 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: The model achieved an ROC-AUC of 0.91 on the ricin tiling dataset.
source: we also tested our ability to predict the performance of sgRNAs in our previously published data set in which we tiled every target site around the TSS of 49 genes known to modulate resistance or sensitivity to the toxin ricin (Gilbert et al., 2014) and obtained an ROC-AUC of 0.91 (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: The position relative to the TSS, including both distance from the TSS and avoidance of canonical nucleosome-occupied regions, most influenced the predicted scores.
source: Overall, the predicted scores were most influenced by the position relative to the TSS, including both distance from the TSS and avoidance of canonical nucleosome-occupied regions (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by feature contribution analysis in Figure 1C

claim: The nucleosome-deprived region immediately downstream of the TSS yielded the strongest predicted activity by SVR.
source: In particular, the nucleosome-deprived region immediately downstream of the TSS yielded the strongest predicted activity by SVR, likely due in part to the contribution of dCas9 directly interfering with early transcriptional initiation or elongation (Gilbert et al., 2013; Qi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by SVR analysis and citations

claim: Guanine directly downstream of the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) is disfavored for sgRNA activity.
source: Sequence features also represented a large contribution to the model, and salient relationships included the disfavoring of guanine directly downstream of the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) which recapitulated previous findings (Doench et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by machine learning analysis and citations

claim: sgRNA secondary structure as predicted by ViennaRNA contributed to the prediction.
source: Additional parameters that contributed to the prediction, included sgRNA secondary structure as predicted by ViennaRNA (Doench et al., 2016; Lorenz et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by feature analysis and citations

claim: The CRISPRa linear regression model had good predictive value with an ROC-AUC of 0.70.
source: While the input set was significantly smaller than for CRISPRi, the resulting linear regression still had good predictive value (ROC-AUC 0.70; Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: The periodic relationship between distance to the TSS and sgRNA activity was less pronounced for CRISPRa than for CRISPRi.
source: We observed that periodic relationship between distance to the TSS and sgRNA activity was less pronounced for CRISPRa than for CRISPRi (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by SVR analysis shown in supplementary figures

claim: sgRNA activity generally correlates across different CRISPR activation strategies.
source: while several strategies have been described for CRISPR-mediated activation (Chavez et al., 2015; Gilbert et al., 2013; Hilton et al., 2015; Konermann et al., 2015; Maeder et al., 2013; Perez-Pinera et al., 2013; Tanenbaum et al., 2014; Zalatan et al., 2015), a recent comparison of these strategies observed that sgRNA activity generally correlated across all approaches (Chavez et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chavez et al., 2016

claim: Approximately 50% of CRISPRi sgRNAs targeting essential genes in the Evers et al. library were inactive.
source: Underscoring the importance of this goal, Evers et al. generated a small-scale CRISPRi library targeting predetermined sets of essential and non-essential genes and conducted screens for growth phenotypes in the bladder carcinoma cell line RT-112, and found that ~50% of the CRISPRi sgRNAs targeting essential genes were inactive (Evers et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Evers et al., 2016

claim: Predicted activity correlated well with sgRNA growth phenotypes in the Evers et al. screen (Pearson R = −0.58, p<10–37).
source: Despite the screen being performed with an independently designed library, using an sgRNA constant region we have found to underperform our current design (Chen et al., 2013), and in a cell type not evaluated in any of our training or test datasets, predicted activity correlated well with the sgRNA growth phenotypes observed in the screen (Figure 3A; Pearson R = −0.58, p<10–37).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: Over 87% of sgRNAs with predicted activity score less than 0.4 were inactive in the Evers et al. screen.
source: Over 40% of the sgRNAs in this library had a predicted activity score less than 0.4, a regime in which the vast majority (over 87%) of sgRNAs were inactive, as defined by z-score > −2 relative to non-essential gene-targeting sgRNAs
evidence: Supported by analysis of Evers et al. data

claim: 77% of sgRNAs with predicted activity scores ≥0.6 in the Evers et al. library are active.
source: By contrast, of the sgRNAs in that library with predicted activity scores ≥0.6, 77% are active.
evidence: Supported by analysis of Evers et al. data

claim: The top 5 sgRNA/gene hCRISPRi-v2 library contained 80% active sgRNAs at 5% false positives.
source: This analysis showed that hCRISPRi-v2 was greatly enriched for active sgRNAs (Figure 3B), and in particular the top 5 sgRNA/gene library contained 80% active sgRNAs at 5% false positives, comparable to the pilot nuclease library tested by Evers et al.
evidence: Supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: The hCRISPRi-v2 library recalled over 91.2% of the gold standard essential genes at 95% precision.
source: In this analysis, the hCRISPRi-v2 library recalled over 91.2% of the gold standard essential genes at 95% precision compared to 81.5% in CRISPRi v1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by precision-recall analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: The precision-recall of the top 5 sgRNA/gene half library was essentially identical to the full 10 sgRNA per gene library.
source: We also found that the precision-recall of the top 5 sgRNA/gene half library was essentially identical to the full 10 sgRNA per gene library.
evidence: Supported by precision-recall analysis

claim: Many genes neighboring the BCR-ABL translocation show K562-specific essentiality mediated by non-specific toxicity of CRISPR-induced double-stranded breaks in the amplified locus.
source: We were also intrigued by the observation by Wang and colleagues of K562-specific essentiality of many genes neighboring the BCR-ABL translocation, which they demonstrated to be mediated by non-specific toxicity of CRISPR-induced double-stranded breaks in the amplified locus (Wang et al., 2015; Wu et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al. and Wu et al.

claim: Similar non-specific toxicity effects have been observed across a range of cancer cell lines.
source: This toxicity appears to be pervasive as similar effects have been observed across a range of cancer cell lines (Aguirre et al., 2016; Munoz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aguirre et al. and Munoz et al.

claim: Few CRISPRi sgRNAs in the BCR amplicon region (other than BCR itself) elicited growth defects.
source: When we compared the phenotypes of CRISPRi sgRNAs to CRISPR nuclease at the BCR amplicon, with all phenotypes standardized to the distribution of negative controls to facilitate comparison, we found that sgRNAs targeting BCR were strongly depleted in both screens, as expected based on the critical role of the BCR-ABL fusion in this cancer cell line (Naumann et al., 2001), but few other CRISPRi sgRNAs in the region elicited growth defects (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: CRISPR nuclease sgRNAs targeting the non-essential gene set were generally depleted relative to negative controls or chromosome Y-targeting sgRNAs.
source: We also found that CRISPR nuclease sgRNAs targeting the non-essential gene set were generally depleted relative to negative controls or chromosome Y-targeting sgRNAs, which should have no targets in the female-derived K562 cell line (Klein et al., 1976)
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation

claim: Cas9 nuclease activity can lead to measurable toxicity not related to the function of individual genes but instead due to the formation of on-target DNA double strand breaks.
source: suggesting that in a CRISPR screen Cas9 nuclease activity can lead to measurable toxicity not related to the function of individual genes but instead due to the formation of on-target DNA double strand breaks, even with alleles present only at 2–3 copies (Naumann et al., 2001).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and citation

claim: CRISPRi did not exhibit generic toxicity at non-essential genes.
source: CRISPRi did not exhibit this generic toxicity at non-essential genes, allowing for detection of genes with subtle phenotypes relative to negative controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The hCRISPRa-v2 screen identified 540 genes that modify robust growth rates upon overexpression, 257 more than the v1 screen.
source: Our hCRISPRa-v2 screen identified 540 genes to modify robust growth rates upon overexpression, 257 more than our previous CRISPRa screen (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 10).
evidence: Supported by experimental screen data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The top categories in DAVID analysis of the v1 screen received ~3-fold greater enrichment scores in the hCRISPRa-v2 hits.
source: the top categories in DAVID analysis of the v1 screen (Huang et al., 2009), enrichment for transcription factor genes (in particular homeobox and forkhead box transcription factors), received ~3-fold greater enrichment scores in the hCRISPRa-v2 hits (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by DAVID analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: 69.3% of sgRNAs in hCRISPRa-v2 with 5 sgRNAs/gene were highly active for genes that were hits in both v1 and v2 screens, versus 45.1% in CRISPRa v1.
source: Analysis of the sgRNA growth phenotype (γ) scores for genes that were hits in both v1 and v2 screens showed that a greater fraction of sgRNAs were highly active (69.3% in hCRISPRa-v2 with 5 sgRNAs/gene versus 45.1% in CRISPRa v1; Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by sgRNA activity analysis

claim: CRISPRi and CRISPRa identified non-overlapping sets of genes that modify robust growth.
source: Finally, we compared the growth phenotypes from hCRISPRi-v2 to hCRISPRa-v2 and found that the two methods identified non-overlapping sets of genes that modify robust growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), consistent with our previous results and highlighting the complementary information provided by these two approaches.
evidence: Supported by comparison of screen results

claim: FANTOM TSS annotations are more accurate than Ensembl/GENCODE annotations for CRISPRi/a sgRNA design.
source: An important improvement was the use of FANTOM consortium annotations instead of Ensembl/GENCODE to define the TSS (Cunningham et al., 2015; FANTOM Consortium and the RIKEN PMI and CLST (DGT) et al., 2014; Harrow et al., 2012) (Supplementary file 2), a finding also recently reported by Radzisheuskaya and colleagues (Radzisheuskaya et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations and improved performance with FANTOM annotations

claim: The CRISPRa activity score dataset contains 2,898 sgRNAs from 9 CRISPRa screens.
source: Due to the requirement for CRISPRa targeting to be upstream of the TSS for maximal activity (Gilbert et al., 2014), we collected an activity score dataset of 2,898 sgRNAs from 9 CRISPRa screens (Y.C. and M.K., personal communication) to train an independent predictive model (Figure 2A).
evidence: Directly stated description of the CRISPRa training dataset

claim: CRISPRa requires targeting upstream of the TSS for maximal activity.
source: Due to the requirement for CRISPRa targeting to be upstream of the TSS for maximal activity (Gilbert et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gilbert et al., 2014

claim: The CRISPRa-v2 libraries are likely to serve as a valuable resource for effectively targeting most activator systems.
source: Our CRISPRa-v2 libraries are thus likely to serve as a valuable resource for effectively targeting most activator systems.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation of sgRNA activity across different activation strategies

claim: CRISPRi and CRISPRa have been shown to be effective for repressing and activating transcription of non-coding genes.
source: While the libraries described here target genes annotated as protein-coding, CRISPRi and CRISPRa have been shown to be effective for repressing and activating transcription of non-coding genes as well (Gilbert et al., 2014; Luo et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The v2 sgRNA prediction algorithms may enable the design of libraries to systematically manipulate expression of non-coding transcripts.
source: Our v2 sgRNA prediction algorithms may enable the design of libraries to systematically manipulate expression of these transcripts as well.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential application

claim: Combining CRISPRi and CRISPRa with methods for robustly expressing multiple sgRNAs will allow for simultaneous control of several genes.
source: Furthermore, combining CRISPRi and CRISPRa with methods for robustly expressing multiple sgRNAs (Kabadi et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2016; Zalatan et al., 2015) will allow for simultaneous control of several genes, facilitating dissection of cellular pathways and systematic mapping of mammalian genetic interactions (Bassik et al., 2013; Costanzo et al., 2010; Schuldiner et al., 2005).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citations to relevant methods

claim: Increased quantitative understanding of factors dictating (d)Cas9 activity and specificity will greatly enhance the expanding set of CRISPR-mediated technologies.
source: Broadly, increased quantitative understanding of the factors dictating (d)Cas9 activity and specificity will greatly enhance the expanding set CRISPR-mediated technologies for controlling gene expression (Hilton et al., 2015; Perez-Pinera et al., 2013; Vojta et al., 2016), imaging targeted loci (Chen et al., 2013; Shao et al., 2016), or precisely editing the genome (Komor et al., 2016; Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: General statement supported by citations to various CRISPR technologies

claim: The model was trained using elastic net linear regression.
source: We used this set as training data for elastic net linear regression (Figure 1A) (Hui Zou, 2005).
evidence: Directly stated in methods description

claim: Categorical and non-linear parameters were binned prior to linear regression.
source: As many of the features included in the model were nonlinear with activity, we first adapted each feature set according to its relationship with activity. Categorical and non-linear parameters were binned prior to linear regression.
evidence: Directly stated in methods description

claim: The relationship between CRISPRi activity and target site distance from the TSS was highly periodic and asymmetric.
source: Because the relationship between CRISPRi activity and target site distance from the TSS was highly periodic and asymmetric, as we had recently shown (Horlbeck et al., 2016), we fit sgRNA positioning features using support vector regression (SVR) to predict a continuous function for any target site (Supplementary Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation and SVR analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: Support vector regression (SVR) was used to fit sgRNA positioning features.
source: we fit sgRNA positioning features using support vector regression (SVR) to predict a continuous function for any target site (Supplementary Figure 1).
evidence: Directly stated in methods description

claim: The hCRISPRi-v2 library includes separate pools for the top 5 and next-best 5 predicted sgRNAs per gene.
source: In addition, we cloned the library as separate pools for the top 5 and next-best 5 predicted sgRNAs per gene to facilitate screens where a smaller library may be advantageous
evidence: Directly stated in library design description

claim: The libraries were divided into 7 thematic sublibraries based on previous divisions of shRNA libraries.
source: and further divided the pools into 7 thematic sublibraries based on our previous divisions of shRNA libraries (Kampmann et al., 2015) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Directly stated in library design description with citation

claim: The CRISPRa model generally shared features with the CRISPRi model.
source: While the input set was significantly smaller than for CRISPRi, the resulting linear regression still had good predictive value (ROC-AUC 0.70; Figure 2B) and generally shared features of the CRISPRi model (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1–2).
evidence: Supported by feature analysis shown in figures

claim: The reduced dynamic range in the nucleosome-depleted region around the TSS contributed to the less pronounced periodic relationship for CRISPRa.
source: a difference we attributed to the reduced dynamic range in the nucleosome-depleted region around the TSS, and the smaller number and relatively lower expression of the genes targeted in the CRISPRa training dataset.
evidence: Inferred explanation for observed difference

claim: The hCRISPRa-v2 library was partitioned into 14 sublibraries.
source: The hCRISPRa-v2 library was partitioned into 14 sublibraries as described for the v2 CRISPRi library above (Figure 2E).
evidence: Directly stated in library design description

claim: Predicted activity for hCRISPRi-v2 was highly correlated with activity, with a Pearson R of 0.56 (p<10–296).
source: Predicted activity was highly correlated with activity, with a Pearson R of 0.56 (p<10–296).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: Predicted activity for hCRISPRa-v2 was highly correlated with activity, with a Pearson R of 0.41 (p<10–38).
source: Predicted activity was highly correlated with activity, with a Pearson R of 0.41 (p<10–38).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: The Wang et al. K562 CRISPR nuclease screen recalled 78.7% of essential genes at 95% precision.
source: This screen recalled somewhat fewer (78.7% vs 90.8%) essential genes at 95% precision than our v2 library screen (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by precision-recall analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: The hCRISPRi-v2 library has a low false negative rate with few false positives.
source: Together, these results indicate that our hCRISPRi-v2 library has a low false negative rate with few false positives
evidence: Inferred from precision-recall analysis

claim: The enrichment for highly active sgRNAs enables robust detection of phenotypes even with a compact library.
source: and the enrichment for highly active sgRNAs enables robust detection of phenotypes even with a compact library.
evidence: Inferred from the performance of the 5 sgRNA/gene library

claim: The BCR-ABL fusion plays a critical role in the K562 cell line.
source: sgRNAs targeting BCR were strongly depleted in both screens, as expected based on the critical role of the BCR-ABL fusion in this cancer cell line (Naumann et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to Naumann et al., 2001

claim: K562 is a female-derived cell line.
source: chromosome Y-targeting sgRNAs, which should have no targets in the female-derived K562 cell line (Klein et al., 1976)
evidence: Supported by citation to Klein et al., 1976

claim: The vast majority of sgRNAs targeting essential genes showed a clear separation from the non-essential gene distribution.
source: Importantly, however, the vast majority of sgRNAs targeting essential genes showed a clear separation from the non-essential gene distribution (Figure 3E), demonstrating the high degree of sensitivity for detecting loss-of-function phenotypes with both CRISPR nuclease and CRISPRi screens.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Both CRISPR nuclease and CRISPRi screens demonstrate high sensitivity for detecting loss-of-function phenotypes.
source: demonstrating the high degree of sensitivity for detecting loss-of-function phenotypes with both CRISPR nuclease and CRISPRi screens.
evidence: Inferred from the clear separation of essential gene-targeting sgRNAs

claim: The v1 and v2 CRISPRa screens showed good agreement.
source: Beyond these additional hits, the v1 and v2 screens showed good agreement (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by comparison shown in supplementary figure

claim: Several genes identified in the hCRISPRi-v2 screen but not in v1 could be attributed to the use of the CAGE-based FANTOM5 TSS annotation.
source: In addition, as with our CRISPRi results, several genes identified in the hCRISPRi-v2 screen but not in v1, including hematopoietically-expressed homeobox HHEX and forkhead box C1 FOXC1, could be attributed to the use of the CAGE-based FANTOM5 TSS annotation (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by genome browser tracks showing TSS annotations

claim: The CRISPRi v1 library identified 1,408 essential genes.
source: While in both screens fewer than 0.21% of these negative control genes scored as hits by these criteria, representing a ~2% empirically estimated false discovery rate overall, we could confidently identify 2,150 essential gene hits in the v2 screen while our v1 screen identified 1,408 essential genes (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by volcano plot analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Fewer than 0.21% of negative control genes scored as hits in both v1 and v2 screens.
source: While in both screens fewer than 0.21% of these negative control genes scored as hits by these criteria, representing a ~2% empirically estimated false discovery rate overall
evidence: Supported by analysis of negative control genes

claim: The empirically estimated false discovery rate is approximately 2%.
source: representing a ~2% empirically estimated false discovery rate overall
evidence: Calculated from negative control gene analysis

claim: Many hit genes exhibited much stronger p-values in the hCRISPRi-v2 screen compared to v1.
source: Many hit genes exhibited much stronger p-values, including a substantial fraction that reached the optimal p-value obtainable in the Mann-Whitney test, indicating that the phenotypes of all targeting sgRNAs for these genes were more pronounced than any of the 3,790 non-targeting control sgRNAs.
evidence: Supported by volcano plot analysis

claim: A substantial fraction of hit genes reached the optimal p-value obtainable in the Mann-Whitney test.
source: including a substantial fraction that reached the optimal p-value obtainable in the Mann-Whitney test, indicating that the phenotypes of all targeting sgRNAs for these genes were more pronounced than any of the 3,790 non-targeting control sgRNAs.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of screen data

claim: The phenotypes of all targeting sgRNAs for genes reaching optimal p-value were more pronounced than any of the 3,790 non-targeting control sgRNAs.
source: indicating that the phenotypes of all targeting sgRNAs for these genes were more pronounced than any of the 3,790 non-targeting control sgRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from the optimal p-value result

claim: The CRISPRi v1 library recalled 81.5% of gold standard essential genes at 95% precision.
source: In this analysis, the hCRISPRi-v2 library recalled over 91.2% of the gold standard essential genes at 95% precision compared to 81.5% in CRISPRi v1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by precision-recall analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: The 5 sgRNA/gene CRISPRi library represents a compelling tool for applications such as cell sorting-based screens or in vivo screens.
source: Therefore, the 5 sgRNA/gene CRISPRi library represents a compelling tool for applications such as cell sorting-based screens (Liberali et al., 2015), or for in vivo screens where cell engraftment and library representation may represent a limiting factor (Braun et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the performance of the 5 sgRNA/gene library with citations to relevant applications

claim: The hCRISPRi-v2 library showed comparable or greater discrimination than other recent genome-scale growth screens in precision-recall analysis.
source: We found that our CRISPRi v2 library showed comparable or in many cases much greater discrimination (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by precision-recall comparison shown in supplementary figure

claim: The improvement in sgRNA activity was due to the significant reduction in the number of inactive sgRNAs rather than any difference in noise.
source: This improvement was due to the significant reduction in the number of inactive sgRNAs rather than any difference in the noise as assessed by the background distribution of non-essential gene-targeting sgRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of sgRNA distributions shown in supplementary figure

claim: The difference in sgRNA phenotypes between v1 and v2 libraries for VCP was likely attributable to the transition from Ensembl to FANTOM as the TSS annotation source.
source: In some instances, as with the known essential gene VCP, the difference in sgRNA phenotypes between v1 and v2 libraries was likely attributable to the transition from Ensembl to FANTOM as the TSS annotation source (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) (Cunningham et al., 2015; FANTOM Consortium and the RIKEN PMI and CLST (DGT) et al., 2014; Harrow et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by genome browser tracks and citations

claim: The lower fraction of effective sgRNAs in previous libraries was a result of the algorithm and the TSS annotation used rather than any intrinsic limitation of CRISPRi.
source: Taken together, the above observations indicate the lower fraction of effective sgRNAs in previous libraries was a result of the algorithm and the TSS annotation used rather than any intrinsic limitation of CRISPRi.
evidence: Inferred from the improved performance with better algorithms and annotations

claim: The greatly improved sgRNA prediction and lack of non-specific toxicity make CRISPRi a state-of-the-art approach for loss-of-function studies.
source: We believe that the greatly improved sgRNA prediction and lack of non-specific toxicity due to nuclease activity, combined with our previous findings that CRISPRi enables inducible, reversible, and homogenous manipulation of gene expression (Gilbert et al., 2014; Mandegar et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2013), make CRISPRi a state-of-the-art approach for loss-of-function studies.
evidence: Inferred from the combined advantages of CRISPRi with citations

claim: Predicted activity for hCRISPRi-v2 sgRNAs targeting essential genes in the K562 screen correlated with predicted activity (Pearson R = −0.42, p<10–21).
source: We found that the hCRISPRi-v2 sgRNA growth phenotypes targeting the Evers et al. essential gene sets correlated with predicted activity as above (Figure 3A; Pearson R = −0.42, p<10–21)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: Designing libraries based on the top predicted scores selected for highly active sgRNAs.
source: and therefore designing the libraries based on the top predicted scores selected for highly active sgRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between predicted activity and empirical activity

claim: Over 60% of inactive sgRNAs can be eliminated a priori by applying a predicted activity threshold of 0.4.
source: enabling a priori elimination of 60% of the inactive sgRNAs by simply applying this threshold.
evidence: Calculated from the analysis of Evers et al. data

claim: 77% of sgRNAs with predicted activity scores ≥0.6 in the Evers et al. library are active.
source: By contrast, of the sgRNAs in that library with predicted activity scores ≥0.6, 77% are active.
evidence: Calculated from the analysis of Evers et al. data

claim: Use of the improved sgRNA constant region would be expected to further increase the fraction of active sgRNAs.
source: Use of the improved sgRNA constant region would be expected to further increase this fraction (Chen et al., 2013; Dang et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citations
